parsed.hook: Woodruff Vineyard sits on the western slopes of the Santa Cruz Mountains where fractured shale and sandstone soils meet Pacific fog funneling through coastal gaps — a site that produces Pinot Noir with more grip and mineral tension than most of what comes out of this AVA. Wind Gap, Pax Mahle's whole-cluster and minimal-intervention project, treats this vineyard as a vehicle for site transparency rather than winemaker ego.
parsed.wine_summary:
Wind Gap was Pax Mahle's second label, launched to explore cool-climate California sites with a lighter touch than his earlier, more extracted Pax wines. The Woodruff Vineyard bottling channels the Santa Cruz Mountains' particular combination of marine-cooled elevation and ancient seabed soils into a Pinot Noir that leans savory and structural rather than fruit-forward. Mahle's approach — native yeast fermentation, whole-cluster inclusion, neutral oak — strips away the winemaker's thumbprint and lets the vineyard's geology do the talking.

The Santa Cruz Mountains AVA remains one of California's most undervalued Pinot Noir sources, overshadowed by Sonoma Coast and Santa Rita Hills despite having older vines, more geological diversity, and a longer track record with the grape. Wind Gap's Woodruff bottling is a case study in why this region deserves more attention: the wine delivers complexity and site specificity at a price point that would be impossible from more fashionable appellations.
parsed.terroir_expression: Woodruff Vineyard's position on the western Santa Cruz Mountains slopes exposes it to direct Pacific influence — fog rolls in through mountain gaps, keeping morning temperatures cool and extending the growing season significantly. The fractured shale and sandstone soils, remnants of ancient seabed uplift, drain rapidly and force vine roots deep into mineral-rich substrate. This stress shows up in the glass as a persistent saline-mineral thread running beneath the fruit, with the kind of iron-tinged earthiness you get from thin, rocky soils where vines can't coast on water or nutrients. The elevation above the fog line means afternoon sun intensity is real, which gives the wine enough ripeness to balance that structural austerity.
parsed.vinification_summary: Mahle's approach at Wind Gap centers on whole-cluster fermentation — meaning a significant portion of grape bunches go into the fermenter with stems intact, which adds tannin structure, herbal complexity, and a spicy aromatic lift that destemmed fruit alone can't achieve. Native yeast drives fermentation, introducing more microbial complexity and a longer, less predictable ferment. Aging in neutral French oak barrels (barrels that have been used multiple times, so they contribute texture and micro-oxygenation without imparting vanilla or toast flavors) keeps the focus on fruit and site character. The result is a wine that feels more Burgundian in its restraint than Californian in its generosity.
